familiar.text: And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.

modern.text: And Jabez called out to the God of Israel, “If only You would bless me and enlarge my territory! May Your hand be with me and keep me from harm, so that I will be free from pain.” And God granted the request of Jabez. More Descendants of Judah

translation_notes: Jabez's prayer is a single narrative, not a guaranteed prosperity formula, territorial entitlement, or method for forcing Divine blessing.
His mother's labor pain is remembered in his name; childbirth pain must not be treated as maternal failure, curse, or destiny for the child.
The request for enlarged border must be read beside verses 39-43, where pastoral expansion becomes displacement and killing.
Hazzelelponi, Helah, Naarah, Bithiah, an unnamed mother in verse 17, and other women interrupt the male-dominant list; omissions remain ethically significant.
Bithiah, daughter of Pharaoh, is incorporated into Judah's memory, resisting ethnic purity narratives.
Artisans, linen workers, potters, farmers, and people working for the king sustain the economy. Royal association may include dependence or coerced labor and should not be romanticized.
Verse 41 describes seizure of peaceful pasture and destruction of inhabitants. Herem/devotion language does not make displacement or killing morally clean.
Verse 43's Amalek reference may never be used against any living people or modern political enemy.
Several names, kinship links, and place identifications are textually uncertain.
safety_note: Reject prosperity-gospel formulas, territorial expansion theology, anti-Black misuse of Ham, ethnic cleansing, genocide, modern Amalek labeling, and romanticized royal labor. The quiet inhabitants displaced for pasture are not disposable background characters.
